label: Actual Conflict Duration
description: The realized duration of active hostilities measured from the February 28 initiation of US/Israel strikes. As of March 29, the conflict has been active for 30 days with no ceasefire in place. Trump's April 6 energy-strike pause deadline creates a near-term inflection point: if Iran does not accept terms, the US has signaled escalation to energy infrastructure targeting. The deadlocked ceasefire negotiations, Houthi entry into the war, and Hezbollah's active operations against Israel all point toward prolonged conflict. Historical reference: the 1991 Gulf War's combat phase lasted 43 days; Operation Iraqi Freedom's major combat phase was 21 days; but asymmetric wars involving proxy networks (Lebanon 2006, Yemen 2015-present) extend for months or years. The decisive US military advantage shortens the conventional phase but proxy activation extends the overall timeline. Under 6 weeks would require Iran accepting terms before or shortly after April 6; 2-4 months reflects a grinding campaign with eventual negotiated halt; beyond that, the conflict has metastasized into a multi-front regional situation.

source.citation: RAND 'War Termination in US Military Operations' 2022; Brookings 'How Wars End' 2024; Crisis Group 'Iran Conflict Duration Assessment' March 2026; IISS Armed Conflict Survey 2025

label: Ceasefire Mechanism
description: The primary mechanism through which hostilities are halted, if at all. Observed: a two-week ceasefire was agreed on April 7-8 through Pakistan mediation (not Turkey as previously expected); the 'turkey_mediated_deal' category now represents any third-party mediated deal (Turkey, Pakistan, or similar). The ceasefire included terms for Hormuz reopening and nuclear talks, but Iran did not honor the Hormuz terms, direct US-Iran negotiations in Islamabad collapsed on April 12 after 21 hours, and on April 13 the US imposed a naval blockade on Iran. On April 21, hours before the April 22 expiration, Trump unilaterally extended the ceasefire at Pakistan's request — Vance-led Islamabad-2 had just dissolved when Iran refused to attend. The character of the active ceasefire has therefore shifted from third-party-mediated deal toward unilateral extension with mediation cover. Within hours of the extension, Iran seized two ships in the strait, and on April 23 Trump ordered the Navy to 'shoot and kill' Iranian mine-layers. The nuclear question (US wants 20-year enrichment ban; Iran offers 5) remains the structural sticking point.

source.citation: Reuters 'US-Iran ceasefire agreed via Pakistan mediation' April 2026; NPR 'Pakistan talks collapse after 21 hours' April 12, 2026; TIME 'Trump extends Iran ceasefire' April 21, 2026; Al Jazeera 'Trump orders shoot-and-kill on Iranian mine-layers' April 23, 2026; Crisis Group 'Ceasefire Mechanisms in the US-Iran Conflict' March 2026

label: Strait of Hormuz Reopening
description: The timeline and manner in which the Strait of Hormuz is reopened to commercial shipping after its closure since March 4. Hormuz handles approximately 20% of global oil transit (~21 million barrels/day). The April 7 ceasefire required reopening but Iran did not comply; on April 13 the US Navy began a counter-blockade of Iranian ports under Adm. Brad Cooper at CENTCOM. A brief April 17 window saw Iran declare the strait open and six cruise ships transit, but Iran re-closed the strait on April 18 citing US 'breaches of trust.' On April 19 Iran's parliament moved to formalize a toll regime banning 'hostile' country ships. By April 23 Trump expanded blockade scope so that no ship may enter or leave the strait without US Navy approval, and ordered the Navy to 'shoot and kill' Iranian mine-layers. By early May, the US launched 'Project Freedom' to escort vessels, leading to direct military clashes, though this was paused by May 6 for Pakistan-mediated talks. Industry consensus as of May 7 (Dallas Fed Energy survey: ~80% of executives; Baker Hughes) remains that the strait will not fully reopen until H2 2026 or later, with oil surging past $113/bbl. By late May (May 22), CENTCOM reported redirecting 97 commercial vessels and disabling four under the maritime blockade since April 13, and the EU expanded sanctions against individuals/entities obstructing Hormuz navigation. Immediate post-ceasefire reopening requires Iranian naval and mine-clearing cooperation that does not exist under blockade conditions. A phased reopening involves US/allied naval escorts and progressive mine-clearing — the 1988 Operation Earnest Will model — but the dual-blockade configuration (Iran blocking Hormuz, US blocking Iranian ports) creates a structurally unstable stand-off. Prolonged closure is now the modal outcome. Permanent rerouting involves expanded use of the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, Saudi east-west pipeline, and UAE Fujairah bypass, but capacity remains capped at well under pre-war Hormuz throughput. Iran's estimated 2,000+ sea mines deployed since March 4 make rapid clearing operationally challenging.

source.citation: CNBC 'Hormuz may not fully reopen until second half of 2026' April 24, 2026; Washington Post 'Project Freedom' May 2026; Bloomberg 'Iran War: When Will the Strait of Hormuz Reopen?' April 21, 2026; Wikipedia '2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis'; Al Jazeera 'Trump orders shoot-and-kill on Iranian mine-layers' April 23, 2026; CENTCOM blockade reports May 22, 2026; EU Council navigation sanctions May 22, 2026; CSIS 'Strait of Hormuz: Strategic Chokepoint Analysis' 2025

label: Iran Post-Khamenei Power Structure
description: The governance outcome in Iran following the confirmed death of Supreme Leader Khamenei in the February 28 strikes. This is unprecedented in the Islamic Republic's 47-year history — the only prior succession (Khomeini to Khamenei in 1989) occurred peacefully with institutional continuity intact. Now, the succession must occur under wartime conditions with degraded command structures, destroyed communications infrastructure, and active foreign military operations. The Assembly of Experts is constitutionally responsible for selecting a new Supreme Leader, but many members are elderly, some may have been killed or displaced, and the body has never operated under war conditions. A hardliner successor (Mojtaba Khamenei, the late leader's son, or Ahmad Khatami) would maintain institutional continuity but lack Khamenei's 35-year authority base. A military junta led by surviving IRGC commanders represents the most likely outcome if civilian institutions fail — the IRGC controls significant economic and military assets independently. A reformist opening requires the war's discrediting of hardliner policies to create space for figures like former foreign minister Zarif or moderate clerics. Fragmented power vacuum is the most dangerous outcome: competing IRGC factions, clerical networks, and regional power centers operating without central authority. Full regime collapse requires sustained military pressure combined with popular uprising — possible but dependent on internal dynamics that external analysis cannot reliably assess.

source.citation: Chatham House 'Iran's Succession Crisis Under Fire' March 2026; CFR 'Post-Khamenei Iran: Governance Scenarios' March 2026; Crisis Group 'Iran Power Structures After the Supreme Leader' 2025; RAND 'Authoritarian Succession in Wartime' 2023

label: US Domestic Political Impact
description: The net domestic political effect of the conflict on US governance and public opinion. A rallying effect reflects the historical pattern of initial public support for military operations — Bush's approval hit 90% after 9/11, 70% after Iraq invasion. Trump's base is solidly supportive but the broader electorate's tolerance depends on duration and casualties. Divided support emerges if the conflict extends beyond the April 6 deadline without clear resolution and economic costs mount through energy prices. Growing opposition materializes if US casualties accumulate, humanitarian imagery dominates media, or the conflict appears open-ended — the Vietnam/Iraq political trajectory. Political crisis represents the most extreme outcome: congressional challenges to war powers, legal challenges to the strike's authorization, and partisan fracture severe enough to constrain military operations. The 2002 AUMF does not cover Iran, and the War Powers Resolution's 60-day clock started February 28, creating a constitutional confrontation by late April if Congress does not authorize continued operations. Trump's use of Article II commander-in-chief authority faces legal challenges that could reach the Supreme Court.

source.citation: Brookings 'Public Opinion and Military Operations' 2025; Gallup 'Presidential Approval in Wartime' historical dataset; CFR 'War Powers and Constitutional Constraints' March 2026; CSIS 'Domestic Politics of Extended Military Operations' 2024

label: War Termination Terms
description: The substantive framework under which hostilities end, ranging from complete Iranian capitulation to a situation where no formal terms exist. Unconditional Iranian surrender is historically rare — even Japan's 1945 surrender retained the emperor — and would require regime collapse or extreme military pressure beyond current operations. Negotiated terms with US advantages is the most likely outcome of a successful ceasefire: Iran accepts nuclear constraints, possibly proxy limitations, in exchange for sanctions relief and implicit regime survival guarantees. Mutual concessions involve face-saving elements for both sides — the JCPOA model where each side claims victory domestically. A frozen conflict produces no terms at all: fighting subsides without formal agreement, leaving all underlying disputes unresolved. The decisive US military balance favors US-advantaged terms, but Iran's asymmetric capabilities through proxies (Hezbollah actively fighting, Houthis entering the war) give it bargaining leverage that pure military balance does not capture. Trump's transactional negotiating style may accelerate a deal but could also produce terms that lack institutional durability.

source.citation: RAND 'War Termination Theory and Practice' 2023; Brookings 'Negotiated Endings to Armed Conflicts' 2024; CFR 'Conflict Termination Frameworks' 2025; Chatham House 'Iran Negotiation Dynamics' March 2026

label: Nuclear Program Verification Outcome
description: The verification and inspection framework for Iran's nuclear program following war termination. The February 28 strikes destroyed declared enrichment facilities at Natanz and Fordow, but IAEA reports indicate Iran's stockpile of 60% enriched uranium (enough for several weapons) is unaccounted for — either destroyed, dispersed, or hidden. Full IAEA access requires Iranian cooperation and a legal framework (either revived Safeguards Agreement or new treaty), which depends on war termination terms. Partial inspection involves limited IAEA presence at declared sites without access to suspected undeclared locations or military dimensions. No verification occurs in frozen-conflict scenarios where Iran rejects all inspection frameworks. A new agreement could go beyond the JCPOA's Additional Protocol to include permanent IAEA presence, military site access, and advanced monitoring — but requires trust-building that the conflict has destroyed. The critical gap: even full IAEA access cannot guarantee detection of covert facilities in a country of 1.6 million square kilometers with extensive tunnel networks. IAEA Director General's March 2026 statement noted the agency has lost all monitoring capability since the strikes.

source.citation: IAEA Board of Governors 'Iran Safeguards Implementation Report' March 2026; Brookings 'Nuclear Verification After Military Strikes' 2025; CSIS 'After the Strike: Iran Nuclear Monitoring Gaps' 2025; Arms Control Association 'JCPOA Lessons for Post-Conflict Verification' 2024

label: Regional Security Framework
description: The institutional framework, if any, that emerges to manage Middle East security in the conflict's aftermath. A US-led new order would build on the Abraham Accords and bilateral defense agreements to create a formal NATO-like structure — the long-discussed 'Middle East Strategic Alliance' (MESA) concept. A UN multilateral framework requires UNSC consensus and broader international buy-in, which is unlikely given Russian and Chinese opposition to US-led outcomes. A GCC-led regional framework reflects the Gulf states' growing assertiveness and could include normalization with a post-Khamenei Iran — the Saudi-Iran March 2023 rapprochement (brokered by China) as a template for post-conflict regional architecture. No framework is the default outcome: historical precedent shows that Middle East conflicts rarely produce durable institutional security architectures. The Abraham Accords' expansion under Trump 1.0 provides the most likely institutional foundation, but whether it can accommodate a post-war Iran or becomes a permanent anti-Iran alliance depends on Iran's regime outcome.

source.citation: CSIS 'Middle East Security Architecture After Iran' 2025; Brookings 'The Abraham Accords and Regional Order' 2025; CFR 'Gulf Security in a Post-War Middle East' March 2026; RAND 'Institutional Frameworks for Regional Stability' 2024

label: Iranian Proxy Network Status
description: The operational status of Iran's network of non-state armed allies following the conflict. As of March 29, both Hezbollah and Houthi forces have actively entered the war — Hezbollah is attacking Israel from Lebanon and Houthis are escalating Red Sea and Arabian Peninsula operations. Iraqi Shia militias have conducted attacks on US bases. The proxy network's fate depends critically on conflict duration: a short conflict may leave proxies largely intact (the 2006 model where Hezbollah survived Israeli operations and declared 'divine victory'); a prolonged campaign gives Israel and the US time to systematically degrade proxy capabilities. However, Hezbollah's 150,000+ rocket arsenal and battle-hardened force from Syria represents a qualitatively different threat than other proxies. The Houthis have demonstrated sophisticated anti-ship capability throughout the Red Sea crisis. 'Dismantled' requires sustained ground operations in Lebanon and Yemen that the US is unlikely to undertake. 'Weakened' is the modal outcome under most scenarios. 'Resilient' reflects the historical pattern of proxy networks surviving and adapting to military pressure. 'Emboldened' occurs if Iran's proxies inflict significant costs on Israel/US and can claim a resistance narrative victory.

source.citation: Crisis Group 'Iran's Proxy Network Under Pressure' March 2026; CSIS 'Hezbollah's War Calculus' March 2026; Chatham House 'Houthi Capabilities and Escalation' March 2026; RAND 'Non-State Armed Groups and State Conflict' 2024

label: Post-War Reconstruction Commitment
description: The scale and leadership of international commitment to Iranian reconstruction after hostilities end. A major US-led effort would mirror post-WWII Marshall Plan logic or post-2003 Iraq reconstruction ($60 billion US-led), but Trump's 'America First' orientation and the political optics of rebuilding a country the US just bombed make this unlikely without a compliant successor regime. An international fund could be organized through the World Bank, UNDP, or an ad hoc donor conference — the Syria reconstruction model that has been discussed but never fully funded. Minimal commitment reflects the most likely outcome: limited humanitarian assistance without structural reconstruction investment, the Afghanistan post-2021 pattern. No commitment occurs in frozen-conflict scenarios where the US and Iran remain adversaries. Iran's pre-war GDP of approximately $400 billion and the reported strikes across 26 provinces suggest reconstruction costs in the hundreds of billions. Political willingness to fund reconstruction is inversely correlated with conflict duration and US domestic opposition.

source.citation: Watson Institute 'Costs of War: Reconstruction' 2025; Brookings 'Post-Conflict Reconstruction Commitments' 2024; World Bank 'MENA Reconstruction Framework' 2025; CBO 'Iraq Reconstruction Cost Analysis: Lessons Learned' 2024

label: Coercive Success Probability (Pape)
description: Pape's central finding: airpower achieves ~100% tactical success but near-zero coercive (political) success against states employing asymmetric strategies. Punishment succeeded 0/8 times. Denial succeeded 5/33 times (~15%), but only with ground forces. Iran's asymmetric strategy makes denial impotent without ground presence. April 2026 observed validation: 38 days of air dominance produced zero political concessions, the April 6 deadline passed without Iranian compliance, the 21-hour Islamabad talks collapsed on April 12 over Iran's refusal to forgo nuclear weapons, the second Islamabad round on April 21 dissolved when Iran refused to attend, and Russia's foreign minister Lavrov publicly argued the campaign would push Iran toward actually acquiring a bomb — the canonical Pape counterproductive outcome. The escalation has moved from ultimatum to ceasefire-with-blockade to ship seizures and 'shoot and kill' orders without producing compliance. The 'counterproductive' bin (campaign produces the outcome it sought to prevent) has gained weight relative to 'failed' (campaign simply doesn't produce concessions).

source.citation: Pape, Bombing to Win (Cornell, 1996) — 33-case empirical analysis; Pape, 'Escalation Trap' March 2026; Al Jazeera 'Lavrov: Iran war could push Tehran toward nuclear bomb' April 2026; NPR 'Islamabad talks collapse' April 12, 2026

label: Ground Escalation Initiated (Pape)
description: Pape estimates ~75% probability the US escalates to ground forces when air coercion fails. This is where 'the trap really closes' — an open-ended commitment in a country of 88 million people spanning 636,000 square miles of mountainous terrain.

source.citation: Pape, 'Escalation Trap' March 2026 (~75% estimate); Pape, Bombing to Win Ch. 9-10

label: Ground Operation Feasibility
description: Physical and logistical feasibility of US ground operations in Iran. Iran's geography makes large-scale ground invasion extremely difficult: the Zagros Mountains to the west create a natural fortress, and no neighboring country (Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan) is likely to allow staging of ground forces. The only viable approach is amphibious from the Persian Gulf/Gulf of Oman, which would be extremely costly. A limited operation such as occupying Kharg or Qeshm islands, or the mainland shore of the Strait of Hormuz to de-blockade it, is the maximum the US appears willing to consider. Even limited island/shore operations would face constant Iranian missile and drone attacks. The mountainous terrain and several large deserts make interior operations extremely challenging.

source.citation: RAND 'Iran Geography and Military Operations' 2024; CSIS 'Amphibious Options in the Persian Gulf' March 2026; AP 'US signals limited ground operation possible' March 2026; Kings and Generals conflict analysis March 2026

label: Resolution Type (Summary)
description: The overall characterization of how the conflict resolves. This is the summary node for Phase 7, integrating ceasefire mechanism, war termination terms, and regional expansion dynamics. A decisive US victory requires both military success (largely achieved) and political consolidation through favorable terms — the 1991 Gulf War template. A negotiated settlement reflects the JCPOA-era model of mutual concessions formalized through diplomacy. A frozen conflict is the Korean War/Kashmir template: fighting stops, no resolution occurs, underlying tensions persist indefinitely. A wider regional war represents the worst-case escalation where Houthi entry, Hezbollah operations, and potential Iraqi militia activation transforms the bilateral US-Iran conflict into a multi-theater regional conflagration. As of May 22, the trajectory remains volatile: the active naval blockade (97 ships redirected, 4 disabled), early May clashes during 'Project Freedom', and expanded EU navigation sanctions maintain the wider-war path's weight. However, Pakistan's Army Chief Syed Asim Munir's May 22 arrival in Tehran and Secretary Rubio's signal of 'some slight progress' in Pakistan-mediated talks offer a fragile diplomatic opening for a negotiated settlement, even as the gap on the nuclear question (enrichment ban) remains a structural hurdle.
